canonical_statement: The study evaluates whether score-tile-group precision routing can accelerate long-context dense-attention prefill while retaining model quality relative to uniform INT8 and FP16 attention baselines.
TileMix partitions dense attention into hardware-aligned score tiles and assigns each legal key-tile group to either FP16 or INT8 score computation without removing token interactions.

For each KV head and query-tile row, TileMix packs up to 64 tile-group routing decisions into one 64-bit word and retrieves each decision with a shift-and-mask operation inside the attention inner loop.

The evaluated routing policies are static, data-free spatial templates that determine FP16 versus INT8 execution while causal and sequence-boundary masks independently determine whether interactions are legal.
The primary score path quantizes query and key blocks to signed symmetric INT8 using absmax scaling, with evaluated block sizes of 128 query tokens and 64 key tokens.

INT8-routed score tiles use INT8 Tensor Core multiplication with INT32 accumulation and scale restoration, while FP16-routed tiles use FP16 score computation; both paths enter a shared floating-point score domain before online-softmax updates.

The primary implementation quantizes query and key operands once per attention call, reuses those INT8 operands across routed groups, and includes quantization, scale preparation, routing, rescaling, memory staging, and fused-attention work in reported implementation-level timing.

The evaluation tests long-context retrieval, long-context question answering, prefill efficiency, and numerical behavior on LLaMA 3.2 3B, with appendix extensions to Vicuna-7B, Qwen2-7B, and Qwen2.5-7B.

All throughput experiments use NVIDIA A100 40GB GPUs, batch size 8, three warmup iterations, and five timed iterations under the same model wrapper; reported throughput includes routing and quantization overhead.

On LongEval with LLaMA 3.2 3B, retrieval quality depends on both the fraction of tile groups routed to INT8 and the spatial placement of the groups retained in FP16; row-random and Sparse Transformer layouts retain stronger accuracy at higher INT8 coverage than several other layouts.

canonical_statement: The implementation and reported experiments target forward inference during long-context prefill rather than training or a broad set of decode workloads.
The evaluated mixed-precision kernel uses FP16 and INT8 Tensor Core paths on NVIDIA A100 GPUs; the paper does not evaluate other GPU generations or numerical formats.
The reported routing policies are static templates; the kernel can accept other static or adaptive policies, but adaptive routing is not evaluated in this study.

The main throughput and LV-Eval comparisons do not report confidence intervals or run-dispersion estimates, so the paper does not quantify uncertainty around those benchmark differences beyond the stated timing protocol.

The authors conclude that tile-group precision routing provides a controllable accuracy-efficiency tradeoff for dense long-context attention by varying FP16 and INT8 arithmetic across legal score-tile groups.
The paper states that a TileMix implementation is publicly available in a linked GitHub repository.
